Let me say, however, in the very few remarks that I propose to address to the House, that I congratulate the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) upon the change of heart which he has experienced during the past twelve months. Do I understand my right hon. friend to deny that there has been such a change. Let me say that I hold under my hand the ' Hansard ' of September 24, 1903, a little more than a year ago, when the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in debate on this House, pressed upon the attention of the House many reasons, in his opinion very conclusive, why the granting of a provincial status to the Northwest Territories should be delayed for many years, and I am bound to say that every one of those reasons which at that time presented themselves to the right hon. gentleman as insuperable difficulties in the way of immediately granting provincial autonomy, exist to-day just as strongly as they did then. The view which I am presenting to the House at this moment was suggested by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) in these words :
But the Prime Minister adduced arguments' that were strong no doubt from this point of view that' the Northwest Territories should not. be granted local self-government for many years to come.
What was the right hon. gentleman's response to that ? Did he deny that that was his opinion at that time? No, he responded to the remarks of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) by ejaculating across the floor of the House ' hear, hear.' So therefore I have good reason to congratulate the right hon gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier upon his change of heart, because when I myself on October 14, 1903, moved in this House a resolution declaring that in the opinion of this House, the time had come when the government Sir WH-FRI DLAURIER.
should take this question into immediate consideration, not one member of the government, not the right hon. gentleman himself, nor one of his colleagues ventured to say one single word upon this all-important subject. They put up in their place two or three gentlemen from the Northwest Territories of Canada to argue as strenuously as they could that the granting of a provincial status should not be accorded to these provinces in the immediate future. The resolution which I moved at that time, after reciting the unanimous resolutions passed by the legislature of the Northwest Territories set forth :
That under the provisions of the British North America Act and amending Acts, the people of the several provinces of Canada enjoy large powers of local self-government committed to and exercised by the executive and legislature of each province.
That the time has arrived when the same powers of local self-government should be-granted to the people of the Northwest Territories of Canada and to this end the said representations and prayers contained in the said humble addresses should be taken into immediate consideration and acted upon forthwith.
The only answer from the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues at that time was the answer of contemptuous silence and the putting up, as I have said, of two or three gentlemen from the Northwest Territories to argue that the time had not yet arrived. Well, the right hon. gentleman Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his colleagues required a certain stimulus and that came in due course. But one of the arguments, and perhaps as strong an argument as any that was presented to the House on that occasion, was the absence of the Minister of the Intei'ior. We all very much regret the indisposition of the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton). It has unfortunately happened very often that he has been absent from sessions of this parliament, and we have endeavoured to facilitate the (passage of his estimates through the House in his absence as much as possible. We all regret his indisposition I am sure, and we trust that in the early future and before any considerable progress is made with this Bill, we shall have in this House the presence of the hon. the Minister of the Interior and the benefit of his views with regard to the measure which has been presented by the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier).
But I said that it required a certain stimulus to the right hon. gentleman to enable

him to appreciate the importance of this question. Letters were addressed to him and to members of his government, over and over again, by the Prime Minister of the Northwest Territories of Canada. To these letters an answer was sometimes deigned and sometimes no answer was given for months. Letters were written by the Prime Minister of the Northwest Territories, to the right hon. gentleman who leads the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), on May 19, 1904, and on June 1, 1904. This matter which has been presented to the House this afternoon as a matter of transcendent importance, not only to the Northwest of Canada, but to the people of this country from one end of it to the other, was so little regarded by the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues at that time, that the whole summer passed away without any answer having been vouchsafed to the Prime Minister of the Northwest Territories. It was only in the stress of an election campaign that the right hon. gentleman awoke to the fact that he had not answered those communications. They were written on May 19 and June 1 ; and it was on September 30, after parliament had been dissolved, and when a campaign was actually in progress, that the right hon. gentleman was good enough to remember that he had not given any answer to the Prime Minister of the Northwest Territories. Then the matter seemed to him to possess a little more importance than he had previously considered. I will not deal with his answer now ; there will be a better opportunity later on for dealing with the subjects with which it is concerned. But he did say this
In reference to your letter of .the 1st of June, I do not think I need discuss at length the representations 'which it contains further than to intimate my opinion that circumstances have justified the wisdom of the course adopted by my government in declining to deal finally two years ago with the many important questions involved in the admission of the Northwest Territories into confederation as a province or provinces.
Did not the right hon. gentleman realize, when he wrote that letter, that it was not two years ago, but about 11 months before, that he himself had stood up in this House and voted against the proposal even to consider the question of the admission of the Northwest Territories into the confederation on a provincial basis ? He went on :
Rapid development has taken place in the Northwest Territories luring the intervening period.
Does he not remember that in the course of the debate to which I have referred, we pointed out that that development was not only going on, but might be expected to continue in the near future at even a greater rate ? However, I will not deal with that subject further than to repeat that, in view of what I have brought to the attention of the right hon. gentleman, and apparently
what he himself had forgotten, there is evident in his remarks to-day a marked change from the opinion lie expressed in this House on the occasion to which I have referred, when he voted against the proposal that the request, the unanimous request, of the representatives and the government of the Northwest Territories should be taken into immediate consideration.
Now, I do not propose to discuss the provisions of this Bill in detail to-day. Let me say, however, that I regret very much that t lie government have not seen fit to give to the people of the new provinces that control over the lands of the Northwest Territories which is enjoyed by all the other provinces of Canada. That is a subject which will bear fuller discussion later on, and I do not propose to weary the House with any extended remarks respecting it this afternoon. The only thing which could lie called an argument made by the right lion, gentleman against that proposition was tiiis : he said it might interfere with the ojieration of the policy of the government with respect to immigration. So far as the rest of his argument is concerned, it would have justified the retention by the Imperial government up to the present time of every acre of Crown lands in Canada ; and I was somewhat astonished to hear from the right hon. gentleman, the advocate, in the past at least, of responsible government, the defender of the liberties of the people on some occasions, according to his own view at least, I was astonished to hear from him the views he put forth this afternoon as to the rights of the people of the Northwest Territories in respect of those lands. He knows something of the history of this question. We remember that there were statesmen in Great Britain not many years ago who thought that the public lands not only of Canada but of all the dependencies of the empire should be retained under the control of the home government, and administered not so much for the benefit of the dependency in which they were situate as for the benefit of the whole empire at large. But it was soon found, when it was attempted to put that view in practice, that it was absolutely impracticable-that to the people living in and developing any dependency7 must be entrusted, and might be safely entrusted, the entire control of the public lands within the dependency. The right hon. gentleman spoke of immigration. Does he not know that there is a new Quebec and a new Ontario ? Does he not know that a tide of immigration may be expected to flow, and indeed, I suppose it is now flowing into these portions of eastern Canada ? Will he venture to say that there lias been any obstacle placed against the immigration policy of the government by the governments which administer those provinces ? Is that the ground the right hon. gentleman takes ? Does he speak from experience, or does he

speak from mere surmise 1 I venture to think that he spoke only from surmise this afternoon, and that if he had looked at this question in the light of experience, in the iight of what is happening to-day in Quebec and Ontario, he might very well have modified the provisions of this Bill, and might very well have entrusted to the people of the Northwest Territories exactly the same control over their lands as is enjoyed by the people of the other provinces. I venture to say further that if he was not willing to trust the people, as I would be willing to trust the people, in this regard-if he regarded them as possibly improvident, as was suggested by the Minister of the Interior last session or the session before-if he feared the result, he might at least have given them the control of the public lands within their respective provinces, subject to some such restriction as that which he has proposed in regard to education. If the principle is good in the one case, I do not see why it should not work out fairly well in the other case.
There are other features of the Bill which will undoubtedly invite discussion. The subject which the right lion, gentleman mentioned last, on which he spoke with great eloquence, and in a spirit of forbearance and moderation, will undoubtedly invite discussion. I do not propose to discuss it this afternoon. There is just one thing, however, that I would like to say about it, and that is that I understand that up to the present time there has been really no school question, to use the common expression, in the Northwest Territories of Canada ; and I sincerely trust that on both sides of the House we will not seek to make this a political question in any sense.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

But at the same time let us beware lest any action of ours may create in the Northwest of Canada for all time to come that question which happily has been entirely absent there in the past. I am speaking in all sincerity in regard to this to my right lion, friend. He has quoted the debates which took place in parliament on this subject. He has laid special stress upon the opinion of Mr. Brown. I will not go over his remarks except to say that of course when Mr. Brown regarded this matter as having been settled for all time to come, he did not speak in an absolutely legal sense. I do not understand my right lion, friend to contend that he did. Does he take the position that that is correct in the legal sense ?

speechtext: I take the position that the constitution certainly makes it imperative for us to respect separate schools wherever they exist.

I do not know that I yet quite seize exactly the meaning of my Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
right lion, friend, but there will be opportunities later and better than the present to learn exactly his view's on that point. Of course the constitutional view of the question-^without touching for the moment the wisdom or propriety of what the right hon. gentleman suggests-the constitutional view of the question is perfectly plain. The parliament of Canada, so far as the Northwest Territories are concerned, can absolutely repeal or deal with in any way any provisions it makes.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, The parliament of Canada can repeal the Act regarding the Canadian Pacific Railway with respect to taxation.

Of course it would be dealing there with vested rights, and my right lion, friend is very conservative in that respect. I am not discussing anything excexit the constitutional aspect, and vested rights are not touched in the matter I am presenting to the House at this moment. The right hon. gentleman knows that while the parliament of Canada can amend in any way it sees fit an Act with regard to the Territories, yet the position will be somewhat different after an Act such as the one now proposed has been passed. By the British North America Act of 1871 the parliament of Canada may from time to time establish newr provinces. Section 2 of that Act provides :
The parliament of Canada may from time to time establish new provinces in any territories forming for the time being part of the Dominion of Canada, but not included in any province thereof, and may, at the time of such establishment, make provision for the constitution and administration of any such province and for the passing of laws for the peace, order and good government of such province, and for its representation in the said parliament.
My right hon. friend has taken the ground, both in the letter to which I have referred, and in his speech in parliament, that the parliamentary representation of the new provinces under the Act I have mentioned, would be absolutely the results of the last census. I take issue with him on that point. I think he was mistaken absolutely when he placed that view before the premier of the Territories and advocated it in this House. The parliament of Canada may do what I have just referred to and what is set out in section 2 of the British North America Act of 1871. Then by section 3 of the same statue :
The parliament of Canada may from time to time, with the consent of the legislature of any province of the said Dominion, increase, diminish or otherwise alter the limits of such province, upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed to by the said legislature.
Then by section 6 of the same Act it is provided :
Except as provided by the third section of this Act, it shall not be competent for the par-

liament of Canada to alter the provisions of the last mentioned Act of the said parliament, in so far as it relates to the province of Manitoba, or of any other Act hereafter establishing new provinces in the said Dominion, subject always to the right of the legislature of the province of Manitoba to alter from time to time the provisions of any law respecting the qualification of electors and members of the' legislative assembly, and to make laws respecting elections In the said province.
So that when we are framing this constitution for the new provinces of Canada, we are framing a constitution which in the future cannot be dealt with by this parliament except with the consent of the provincial legislature.
Just one word more. This Bill of course will have to be printed and we shall require some time to consider it and perhaps some further information will require to be brought down. I have made a note of what I think should be brought down for the information of the House before this Bill is further discussed. I would like to direct the attention of my right hon. friend to certain returns moved for on page 119 of the Votes and Proceedings, of which some have not been brought down. I am alluding of course only to those relating to the Northwest Territories. 1 would like also to have from the right hon. gentleman full information as to the centres of population in the new provinces and the course and tendency of immigration since the census of 1901. This is of importance in connection with the establishment of electoral divisions and also with regard to the boundaries of the two provinces. In the next place, I would like to know if possible the quantity of lands which have been patented in the two provinces for homestead purposes, the quantity granted to railway companies or which railway companies, under the terms of their charter, are entitled to select at present. Also what lands have been granted to railway companies, but which have not been earned or patented. And I would like a statement, if it is not already contained in the Bill or the speech of my right hon. friend, of what lands yet remain vested in the Crown. I would like also to know as to these lands, and especially in connection with the proposed boundaries of the two provinces, what proportion is more suitable for the growing of grain, and where it is situated, what proportion is more suitable for ranching or other description of farming and where it is situated, and what proportion is supposed to require irrigation and where situated. All this information will be of value to us in discussing the question of boundaries between the proposed provinces. It would be desirable also that on the second reading of the Bill some definite information should be given to us as to what is the practical condition of education in the Territories at present. I fully expected
to have received that information this afternoon but was disappointed. Also information as to tlie systems of public schools which have been established there and under what ordinances, management and inspection they are carried on. What number of schools, public schools in the ordinary sense, are to be found there and what number of separate schools ? I think that all this information and other information of a kindred character should be placed before the House, and I am sure that upon this question, to which the right hon. gentleman lias alluded with	so	much feeling,	weshall all	endeavour	to meet	him	intiie same	spirit.	I	will not	go	overthe past.	I will	not	allude to	the	fact
that possibly a somewhat different spirit was manifested some eight or nine years ago when a similar question arose. It has been asserted by some-with what truth I know not-that that question Was deliberately brought into the political arena for the advantage it might give to hon. gentlemen on the other side. I will not do more than allude to that and express once more the hope that whatever may have been done in the past by hon. gentlemen opposite, which is not consistent with the lofty ideals my hon. friend has expressed this afternoon, we on this side at least shall not emulate that example, but shall deal with this question in a spirit of Christian charity and forbearance, realizing that on all such questions there are two sides and endeavouring each one of us too realize that we must consider the question presented to us not only from our own standpoint but also from the standpoint of those who differ from us in opinion. It is above all things desirable that these questions and considerations, touching sometimes upon differences of races and dealing with matters of dogma and creed, should not be introduced into the political arena more than is absolutely necessary. I know that the House will deal with this question in that spirit, and I trust and believe that we may find some solution of what has been presented to us this afternoon by the right hon. gentleman which will commend itself generally to the people of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Mr. SPItOTJLE. I do not rise to continue the debate but merely to ask a couple of questions. office-

When that section was previously before the committee, the suggestion was made that the getting of any information by an officer in addition to what was authorized in the schedules given him should be made an indictable offence. I promised to look into that and get the opinion of the law officers. I have done so, and am quite willing that this should be made an indictable offence, and I propose to introduce a new section, section 30 (a) next after this clause, to attain the object desired. I take it that the object of having the section stand has thus been met, and that the section may pass.

I desire to call the minister's attention to another point that was raised during the discussion of this section. I asked the minister to consider what officers would be included in the words of section 30-' every officer, census commissioner, enumerator, agent and other person employed in the execution of this Act,' and to say how his section would work in conjunction with section 17. I understood the minister then to say that probably the descriptive words in section 30 would include all the public officers described in section 17. I did not understand the minister to be positive on that point. It is a matter of some importance, and perhaps the minister will explain what conclusion he came to concerning it.

I did not think it was necessary that officers employed by other authority, who furnish us information under this Act, should be called upon to take an oath under this Act. We would require Mr SPKOULE.
them to say that the information furnished us was what they had collected. But I do not think we could do more than that. They are not acting as officers of the department in any way, except as they supply information to us. But I think when they supply information it should be under some form saying that this was the information they had collected.

I think the minister and the committee should carefully consider the effect of this legislation. As the minister says, some of the information that would be given by these officials would be given merely as information received from other sources, and they would not be able to pledge themselves to the accuracy of it as coining from original sources. But they will be bound, under this section, to swear to Ihe faithful and exact discharge of the duties that are expected of them and to the secrecy of the statistics collected. And under section 31, it is provided that these officials, in case they make a false declaration, will be guilty of an indictable offence. I call the minister's attention again to the position we are taking in connection with sections 17 and 30 taken together. We have certain officials appointed by municipalities or by the provincial government and bound to carry out the instructions of the authority that appointed them. Almost inevitably. 1 fear, at some time, the duties prescribed by the federal government under this Act will conflict with the duties as defined by the local authorities. And it is a pretty drastic measure to provide that a neglect of duty required by this government on the part of an officer appointed by the local government will subject the officer not merely to a fine, but to being declared guilty of an indictable offence. I think we come dangerously near usurping the powers of the local governments ; and, in that view, I think this is not a wise provision.

Section 31 provides that every person employed in the execution of this Act ' who makes wilful default in any matter required of him by this Act, or wilfully makes any false declaration touching any such matter,' is guilty of an indictable offence. Of course, if he makes a return saying that it is information he has collected in his capacity as an officer of the local authority, and wilfully falsifies that return, I think he should be held guilty of an indictable offence. But if he transmits the information he collects, he would carry out the full spirit of the law.

I do not wish to put more difficulties in the way of the Bill than necessarily meet it. Of course, if one makes a false declaration, he is not much to be commiserated in any punishment. But there is another feature. Section 31 says ' ' who makes wilful default in any matter required of him by this Act.' There may be a bona

Patent Record. $17,000.
Are these items covered by the portion of the Auditor General's Report which has been brought down ?
I think the last volume of the Auditor General's Report was laid on the table of the House yesterday.

This is the same item that we have had for several years back, though it has been increasing a little in amount. It is for the publication of the ' Patent Record,' which is published monthly, and which gives the patents issued, with a short outline of their character, and with a print which is supplied along with the application for the patent.
Where are these prints made ?
In the Printing Bureau or through the Printing Bureau. I have nothing to do with that. We simply pay the bills which the Printing Bureau presents to us.
How is that work distributed ?

It is sold to subscribers at the rate of twenty cents per number, it is sent regularly to members of the Senate and House of Commons, and it is distributed gratis to libraries and public institutions, and a large number are sent to Great Britain for distribution there to public libraries and other institutions.
What income do you derive from it ?
I am informed that it amounts to some hundreds of dollars, but it is not a large amount. That goes to consolidated fund.
I suppose it is carried on in exactly the same way as it was formerly ?
Exactly as it has been since I have been in office, except that it is expanding with the larger number of patents issued from year to year.

Would not the issue of this yearly or half-yearly answer every purpose ? Every member receives copies of this publication monthly. I look over them occasionally and try to distribute them, but they receive very little attention. It appears to me that a great deal of the expense, perhaps one-half or two-thirds, might be saved by issuing it quarterly, half-yearly or yearly. I dare say it may be interesting to designers. The illustrations in it are undoubtedly of a most interesting character, but it is a good deal of money to pay, and unless the minister knows that the country is getting value for it, I think it might be well to consider whether some change could not be made in the method of distribution.

I may say that there is a demand on the part of those interested in patents that it should be issued weekly instead of monthly. In the United States the similar publication is issued weekly. It is true, my hon. friend or myself or others who are not specially interested in patent matters, do not require these publications very often ; but those who are taking out patents or have any intention of doing so, as well as patent solicitors and the large body of people who are interested in patents or own patents, and manufacturers who wish to make use of patents in their industries, watch it very closely. The pressure on the department is altogether in the opposite direction from what my hon. friend suggests. I do not think the difference in expense, from issuing it half yearly or monthly, would be very great, because the monthly issues are not bouud, but only stitched, and the printing would have to be done whether they were issued monthlv or half-yearly.
How many are issued ?

I am informed that about
4,000	are printed. We always keep a number in reserve, because very frequently we have applications for back numbers.

Fragmentary statistics are almost more dangerous than none.
Statistical Year-book, $6,000.

The hon. minister will remember that Mr. Ross, of Victoria, who used to take a warm interest in this item, generally laid on the table, when we were discussing it, the year-books of Australia, New Zealand, Natal and the Cape, and my hon. friend will no doubt remember that our own does not compare at all favourably with those issued by those colonies. Is there any prospect of any improvement and of our getting our year-book a little earlier than we have been in the habit of getting it in the past few years ? In the year-books of Australia and the other British dependencies, there are maps showing the lines of railways in those colonies and also other information not to be found in our book. My hon. friend will admit that the year-book comes out in Canada at a very late date. Would it not be possible to have it published a little earlier, which ought to be more easily done now that my hon. friend has established a bureau of statistics. I think also we might have a few more copies of the French translation and have them a little earlier. The French edition conies out very late indeed. The translation is not difficult. It mostly consists of a compilation of figures, and there is a very considerable demand in our own province and outside for a French edition.
I do not think that a few copies more would make much difference in the cost of printing. How many copies will this sum of $0,000 give us?

I hare here the details for 1903. There were then 5,000 copies of the English paper edition and 2,000 bound ; 000 copies of the French paper edition and 300 bound. In that year we took a smaller vote than we did last year and are asking for this year. We are taking an additional $1,000, but the figures for 1903 are the re-



suit of a vote of $5,000. We are asking this year for $6,000, and that extra money will be spent in obtaining so many more copies.
How much per book ?

It is pretty hard to figure that out. About 40 cents, but some are in paper and some bound. The bound ones cost a good deal more than the paper ones.
I can assure my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier that 1 will do my best to have the book out earlier, but it must be borne in mind that the gentleman in charge of the work cannot begin until the reports of the different departments are finished. I am told that probably the book will be ready about May 10, this year. The translation requires to be done by an experienced man, and we have an officer who has been doing that work many years, but I would be very willing to have the work done more rapidlv if that could be accomplished by additional assistance. But there is this difficulty always in the translation. The translators want to work from the proof sheets of the Printing Bureau instead of from the copies. They say that they can finish their work just as quickly in the end if they wait for the proofs as if they worked from the typewritten copies. I could never understand why you cannot translate typewritten copy as well as proof, but they insist that they cannot and insist on waiting until the gal-lev proofs of the English edition are before them. I tried to argue the question with them but they said they knew their business better than I.

I would like my hon. friend to bear in mind what I said with regard to the maps. In the year-books of the other colonies there are maps showing the mineral areas, the agricultural areas, the forest areas and the principal railways. I do not know whether that would materially increase the cost, but it would certainly increase the interest of the work.

I have taken a note of what my hon. friend says. Bet me say that in preparing for the exhibitions, we have had a book compiled very largely from the year book for distribution at these exhibitions. We have had some maps prepared, and I admit that it would be a good thing that we should have maps in the different year-books showing the railroads, forest, mineral areas and so on. Those maps are however, very expensive and would add materially to the cost of the book, and I might have to ask for an additional vote.

Of course, these statistics are useless when they grow old and musty. Though we have the promise that they are to tie put out more promptly in the future, I find, on looking over the list for the last three years, that the publication has been growing later. If we go on in this way they Mr. FISHER.
will soon be oyer a year old before they are made public. In 1900 the publication was on June 22 ; in 1901, on May 15 ; in 1902, May 28 ; and in 1903, June 29. So far as tne municipal authorities are concerned they responded promptly, proving that they are probably the best agency for gathering statistics.
Are the government selling maps such as were distributed amongst members of the House last year 1 A man was in my town recently selling them.

No maps are issued by my department. I suppose the map the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Reid) refers to is one issued by the Department of the Interior a year and a half or two years ago. It was an excellent map and was issued in different sizes. But I do not think the department are selling them.

They are very fine maps.
I got fifty of them and distributed them through my riding. To my surprise a man was selling them around our town.

I think he must have got them surreptitiously. I am sure the department could not countenance anything of that kind. I will call the attention of the Department of the Interior to what the hon. gentleman has said.

Toronto, Oct. 13.
My Dear Aylesworth,-In answer to your communication requesting that there be made without any delays a full and detailed survey and report' showing Id detail the work and the estimated cost of the proposed outlets of the Trent Valley canal at both Port Hope and Trenton, by competent, reliable and impartial engineers -such report and survey to include hydraulic lift locks and also locks of any other design which might be considered or adopted, also electrical power for mechanical and lighting purposes, buoys, cost of operation and maintenance, together with a report on the construction of any railway and highway bridges that may be necessary, also the damages resuiting from obstruction of water, flooding of lands or injuring lands, on other properties on each route, and also including construction and maintenance of all necessary harbour facilities and lighthouses with respect to each route, I beg to say that this subject' has already engaged the attention of the government which some time ago decided that such survey and report of estimated cost should be made. I regret to learn from your letter that the work in question is possibly not proceeding on a satisfactory basis, and beg to lassure you that the government will with all possible speed cause the survey and report which you ask to be made. It is further intended to have such survey and report made with reference not only to a work of the depth and capacity of the completed portion of the Trent Valley canal, but also of a work of greater depth and capacity, and therefore the instructions to the engineers will be given in accordance with such intention. From memory I cannot go more fully into the details of the survey, plans and route. It is the intention of the government to have the most complete inquiries made as to the relative merits of the two routes in all their bearings, and therefore the survey and report in question will be sufficiently comprehensive, not merely to cover details above mentioned, but any other details, which it would be either proper or necessary to know before making the selection of an outlet. If the details of the respective surveys and reports fall short of what is necessary or advisable the government will be glad to supplement them in any manner that you recommend in order to have both the government and the country in full possession of 474
all information touching the relative merits of the various routes before a selection is made.
Yours very truly,
WILFRID LAURIER. To A. B. Aylesworth, Port Hope.
With regard to that letter I may say, Mr. Chairman, that some gentlemen in the town of Port Hope who heard that letter read on the occasion when my hon. friend the Postmaster General, I think, was present, were not quite satisfied with the terms of the letter, and subsequently another one a little stronger in its terms was sent by the right hon. gentleman at the head of the government, I think to Mr. Aylesworth, in which he made it quite clear that the surveys to be made of these two routes should be made on a basis of an 8 feet 4 depth of canal. Now the matter of surprise to me is this, that although at that election there were apparently two routes suggested, those by way of Port Hope and Trenton, now there crops up an additional route by way of Cobourg. I do not know on what ground the hon. minister is having a survey made by way of Cobourg, except that my hon. friend, whom I do not see in his seat this evening, the hon. member (for West Northumberland (:Mi'u McColl) managed to secure his election on that occasion, and naturally there might be some disposition on the part of the government to run a canal through a constituency which was successful in returning a supporter of the government. However that may be, I desire to call the attention of the minister to several facts in connection with the routes by Port Hope and Trenton-I cannot say one word about Cobourg, because I know nothing whatever about that route. But there is this to be said in addition to what I have already brought to the attention of the government on various occasions ; and I think that the right hon. premier of this government might have given me some credit for having brought this matter before the House on various occasions, and considered that I was perhaps a little more worthy of representing the county of Durham from residence reasons, if for no other, than the Hon. Mr. Aylesworth. However, in addition to what I have already brought to the attention of the government, I wish to mention this fact, that taking into consideration the buoying and the lighting of the canal for a distance of forty miles, the excess in length of the canal which would be necessary by way of Trenton, I am informed by gentlemen who have taken this matter into earnest consideration that the extra expense of running a canal by way of Trenton over and above what it would cost by way of Port Hope, would represent a capitalization of a million and a half dollars. I do not desire on this occasion to repeat the arguments that I have brought before the House before on three separate occasions ; but I do wish to impress upon the Minister of Railways and

Canals that no route should be adopted by 1 the government until the most thorough inquiry and examination has taken place, not only by the engineers in charge of the work, but by the minister himself. X think the minister is capable of forming a judgment if he will only go over the ground, and if he does so he will find that the outlet by way of Port Hope is the proper outlet, not only by reason of the comparatively small expense that will be entailed in building the canal by that route, but for many other reasons which could be pointed out to him.
I would like to ask the minister why this survey has been made by way of Cobourg, and why the other two routes by way of Trenton and Port Hope are ignored for the time being ?

I may say to my hon. friend that the survey by way of Cobourg was not undertaken until about the 10th or 12th of December. The object of that survey is to get possession of all the facts relating to the lake entrance of the Trent valley waterway. I regret that it has not been my privilege to go over this waterway and to visit the different sections. I rnuslt, therefore, necessarily discuss the subject, if I undertook to discuss it at all, quite in the dark so far as any personal knowledge of the locality is concerned. I say I regret that I have not had an opportunity of visiting the locality, and I shall certainly avail myself of the earliest possible occasion to go over the entire route of these waterways. There are three possible outlets, one at Trenton, as I understand, where a survey has been made, and where one is now in progress ; another at Port Hope, and another at Cobourg, which was undertaken somewhere about the middle of December.
I hope the minister will not forget the one by Newmarket and Aurora.

That is in another direction, I think. I find a difference of opinion exists as respects these different routes. My hon. friend from Durham (Mr. Ward) will recollect that I brought down and laid on the table of the House last session, I think it was, reports of the engineers with respect to the surveys which had been made in the previous year. He did not seem to be satisfied with those surveys, he thought it would be vex-y much better to have a fuller survey made and more accurate information, from his standpoint. In deference to the views which he expressed at that time, and in deference to the views expi-es-sed by other members, the whole matter was gone into, and the question of surveys of these different routes was placed in charge of Mr. Walsh, a very eminent and competent engineer. I approach this subject with an entirely open mind, I have no preference for one route or the other and I trust that auy arrangement that may be reached in the matter will be reached entirely upon the

merits, because that after all is the important matter. There must be a coi-rect route, or one of the routes must be better than the others. The point is to be able to find out exactly which is the most advantageous to the Trent valley waterway.

My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals has referred to two previous surveys. Now, my whole objection to these suxweys has been this, that they wei-e not made of the two routes upon exactly the same basis. I pointed out last session and the session before, particularly last session, the discrepancies that existed in the survey of Mr. McLeod as to the route by Port Hope and by way of Ti'enton. It will not take a moment to instance two particular branches of the survey which differ entirely as far as the two routes are concerned. In the first place, there are the reaches of the river and the reaches generally of the canal. As my hon. friend will understand, there are nearly forty miles of reaches by the Trent route, between Rice lake and Trenton. If my hon. friend will examine the report of Mr. McLeod, the engineer who made these surveys, he will find that although estimates for 8 feet 4 inches in the canal were made, he states iu another portion of his report that he only estimates for 6 feet in the reaches. He admits that in the canal proper every one of the excavations has to be made in limestone rock and that the excavations in the reaches are in limestone rock also. But there is not one dollar estimated for the excavation of the difference between C feet and 8 feet 4 inches in the reaches of the river or the canal. Therefore, there is a very large sum of money required for excavating these reaches of the river and the canal not included in the estimates of the cost as between Port Hope and Trenton. Another thing which I pointed out to the committee at the time was that there was not one dollar estimated for drowned land. It is well known that there are some 20,000 or 30,000 acres of drowned land already on the route of the canal, and it is intended to raise Chisholm's darn about two feet, which will drown about 10,000 acres more land. But there is not one dollar estimated for the drowning of this extra amount of land, and I say that unless we have an estimate of all these different things, as between the two routes, my hon. friend cannot possibly come to a just conclusion ; and until a satisfactory survey is made, it is utterly impossible, as "far as the cost is concerned, to make a correct choice in the matter.
The cost of drowned lands being a very important factor in the cost of the canal.
Certainly.

That is the section about which there is a doubt as to the route to be adopted. There are two routes when you get to Lake Ontario, one is by way of Port Hope.
You want to get from Heely's Falls to Port Hope.

One route is by way of Trenton and another by way of Port Hope. Another is suggested by way of Cobourg, and still another which has been brought to my attention within the last few weeks or days, by way of Presq'ile harbour.
Then nothing is done in the way of helping navigation from Heely's Falls down to Trenton ?
No.

I have had the privilege of living along the route, and I, am delighted to see that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House are taking an interest in this important waterway. I may inform the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) that the Georgian bay is 580 feet above sea level. From Georgian bay to Lake Couchiching is about thirteen miles.
Why did you not go up by Severn river ?

That is a rocky country and would be quite circuitous. The recommendation I believe is in favour of the direct route across from Lake Couchi-ching and coming in by Waubaushene. Lake Couchiching is 719 feet above the level of the sea. Thence down Lake Simcoe to Game-bridge and then up Talbot river, there Is

some cutting between Simcoe and Balsover. Then coming to Kirkfield there is a lock about 50 feet high. Balsam lake is 838 feet above sea level and is on the height of land. From Balsam lake you pass through Rosedale river into Cameron lake. There is a lock between Balsam lake and Cameron lake at Rosedale of three or four feet. From Cameron lake you pass into Sturgeon lake by two locks twenty-eight feet in height. From Sturgeon lake you pass into Pigeon lake by a lock at Bobcay-geon about six or seven feet high. From Pigeon lake it is a level sail to Buclchorn, where there is a lock. Then you pass into Deer and Lovesick lakes. At Burleigh Falls there are locks entering into Stony lake and Clear lake. Then by Clear lake you pass south to Lakefield and on to Peterborough where you reach the lift-lock From below the lift-lock at Peterboro' there is uninterrupted navigation down to Hastings at the foot of Rice lake, where there is a lock. From Hastings to Heely's Falls there is uninterrupted navigation. There may be some work to be done from Camp-bellford and Chisholm's Rapids down to Trenton, about nine and a half or ten miles, that can be overcome by damming the river. I may point out that at the present moment there is uninterrupted navigation from Kirkfield to Heely's Falls, at least in the summer time. As soon as the locks are completed at Kirkfield there will be uninterrupted navigation from Orillia to Heely's Falls, leaving only the two ends to be completed, and these are the pieces of work I am urging on the minister now to complete.
What is the mileage from Heely's Falls to Lakefield ?

The entire mileage is nearly 200 miles. There is not one foot of cutting except at the western end. There will be no cutting whatever excepting it may be half a mile here and there. It is all the way natural shores where steamers can go full sail ahead.
I am obliged to the minister and to his efficient deputy head on this side of the House for the information.
I would like to ask the minister if it is intended to make any further surveys by way of Trenton before the terminus of the canal is decided upon?

That matter has been brought to my notice so recently that I am not in a position to determine. I have placed the matter in the hands of the chief engineer, and we will have to inquire as to the possibility of that route. It is no use to have a survey there unless there is some prospect of making it available for the purposes of the canal. Of course there Is a resolution of the municipalities favouring it.
Mr, SAM. HUGHES.
Mr. FOSTER, What was it that caused the survey to be started by way of Co-bourg?
Mr. EMJlERiSON. Instructions were given to the chief engineer to study out all these possible outlets of this waterway on Lake Ontario, and the engineer in charge determined that Cobourg was worthy of study.
That was the engineer's initiative.

I would like to mention to the minister that he is a little mistaken in saying that the survey by way of Cobourg was initiated in December. I heard towards the end of October that surveys were going on then at Cobourg.
That is an error. I have a memorandum from the engineer about the commencement.

I heard during the election campaign that the very engineers that were engaged in the survey of the Port Hope route were at the same time making a survey by way of Cobourg. That was the first I heard of it.
Galops canal-to stop leak in hank, $25,000.

This was rendered necessary owing to leaks in the banks. During the construction years ago some cribs were left in the banks of the canal. Since the level has been raised increasing the pressure, the water has forced itself through and along the cribs. The work is done by contract and tender, Mr. O'Leary having the contract.
Mr. ,T. D. REID. I cannot understand exactly how this leak occurred. I remember that there used to be a small leak about that point some years ago, but I understand that that was provided for in the original contract, and that it was supposed to have been well taken care of by the contractors when they were doing that excavation work and strengthening the bank. That bank was raised some six feet all along there.
That increased the pressure according to the report of the engineers and therefore increased the leak.

Of course it increased the pressure, because there were six feet more of water in the canal, but then the contractors were supposed to put in rock and earth sufficient to strengthen the bank and the work could not have been done properly by the contractors when they built that part of the work.
I know that is absolutely necessary and the chief engineer tells me that that was not the cause of the difficulty.

I remember the work going on there at the time and it was sup-

posed to be to strengthen the bank in order to prevent a leak of any kind occurring. My opinion is that that work was not properly done when the contractors were filling in the canal bank.

The chief engineer tells me that the work was properly done in the original construction as far as the making of the bank is concerned and that the leak was the result of the pressure on the renewed bank.
How is that work to be done ?
The crib is to be taken up. That is under contract now and the vote of $25,000 will certainly complete the work.
I asked the hon. minister last year that he should do something with the view of having the bridge at Cardinal properly attended to. Here is the question I asked last year :
Has the minister lone anything about arranging to have the bridge at Cardinal swung by some other means than hand power ?
That matter is receiving the attention of the department now.
It was receiving it a year ago.

I had the papers under consideration this morning, and some instructions were given with a view to having that work done at once, so that the bridge will be swung by electric power.
That is a year ago and still there has been nothing done.

Arrangements were being entered into at that time with the Edwardsburg Starch Company with the view to having the bridge swung that way. That is being carried out and I am in hopes that it will be fully completed so that there will be no further difficulty in that directon.
Will it be completed at an early date ?
We expect it to be completed at a very early date.
Has the contract been let to the Edwardsburg Starch Company ?

There have been some differences between that company and the Department of Railways and Canals, but the whole matter is under negotiation now with the view of settling all these difficulties. They have agreed to do the work for a certain consideration and while the contract has not been actually signed and executed, yet I have no doubt but that it will be fully completed and carried out.

Will the hon. minister state if the item of $26,500 for the Galops
rapids will complete the work or will there be any further votes for that work ?
Nothing more for that.
That finishes it ?

That finishes it.
Cornwall canal-to fill in space between old and new locks at foot of canal, $4,000.
Is that to be done by contract ?
Yes.
$2,000 was voted last year. Has anything been done yet ?
No, nothing has been done. There was nothing voted last year.
That is an error.

What is the intention of the government in so far as that lighting contract is concerned ? Is it the intention of the government to take over the lighting plant and work it themselves or allow it to be continued under the contract which exists ? The government have the power of expropriation. I think the question came up last year.

There are no reasons which suggest themselves to me now why we should undertake to expropriate at this time.
Williamsburg canals-to purchase steam hoist and steam pump, $1,500.
What about that ?
There has never been a steam hoist or a steam pump on the Williamsburg canals and for the heavy work now being done one is necessary.
I think there was an item in the estimates last year for building a new gate lifter. What has been done in regard to that ?
It is being built.
Is the building being built by contract ?
It is being built by contract.
Who has the contract?
I really cannot recall.
The reason I asked is that I have seen no advertisement for that.
The engineer tells me there were advertisements.

What is the minister going to do about that position of collector on the Wallaceburg canal ? I see here at Cardinal the collector got $1,051.51, and last year he did not collect a cent of canal toils.

Later on I will have an opportunity of discussing the matter of collectors. 1 shall probably be in a position to announce the policy of the government as to whether or not we will resume the collection of tolls.
In the meantime' the minister might intimate what this $1,051 was paid for.

That has been explained time and time again. The tolls were abolished for a period of two seasons, but it was necessary to continue the collector's to keep a record of all traffic over the canals with a view to determining the effect of making the canals free, to ascertain whether the traffic was increased by that or not, and generally to determine as to the effect of that policy. That has been in effect for two seasons.
How is the amount arrived at ?

Collectors were paid stated salaries, and they were continued. If the canals are continued free, there will have to be a decision made with respect to these officials.
Murray canal, $18,000.
The minister might explain this.

There are at each side of each end of this canal ten isolated wooden cribs, connected by four stringers and flooring. The cribs are 24 feet apart, making 20 cribs at each end. These cribs and flooring are almost entirely decayed, having been built about twenty years ago. It is proposed to build them of concrete from a height of one foot below low water mark, standing 8 feet above low water mark. The wall is to be 9 feet high, 25 feet 6 inches thick for 5 feet, then 2 feet thick for the balance. The size of the pier is 25 by 30 feet, making 100 yards in each pier. Two piers have already been built out of the appropriation for repairs. Eighteen remain to be done at each end. An appropriation will be asked next year to rebuild the western end in the same way. It seems to be in the interests of economy to have these cribs rebuilt in this way with concrete.
Can the minister state the volume of traffic passing through the Murray canal, and whether it is increasing or decreasing ?
From memory, I would say that last year it was somewhat less than the previous year. There have been some fluctuations, but in the main there has been an increase.
Has the minister an idea of what tonnage goes through that canal ?

I cannot give my hon. friend a statement of that; I do not carry Mr. J. D. REID.
the figures in my mind. I had the general result before me not long since, but I cannot exactly recall it.
' It would be interesting to know whether the trade through that canal has been increased by it.

There has been an increase in the trade, but whether it is true to that canal I am hardly in a position to say.
Welland canal-chargeable to income, $85,000. Stone protection to banks of new canal, $10,000.

There was a vote of $20,000 last year ; $10,000 only was expended, and we are asking for a revote of $10,-
000.
Is any part of the next vote for $30,000 a revote ?

No part of it is a revote. $30,000 was expended last year. This work has been going on from time to time, and it is being done by the canal staff. On the works at Port Dalhousie there was expended, up to December 31, 1904, $50,400, and there yet remains to be done $39,200. The total cost of this work was estimated at $89,000.
What was the income from the Welland canal last year ?
There was no income from the tolls.	.
Then how do you charge it to income ?
It is a fiction ; there is a small income in connection with leases, I think.
The minister says that this work is being done by the canal staff. Are we to understand that there is a regular staff of workmen at all times repairing the canal ?

During the summer season. There are workshops at Port Dalhousie. That has been the system for years. They make the repairs to the gates, and when they have no repairs to do they make new gates to have them on hand.
How many men of that class are regularly employed on the canal J It seems to me that work of this kind should be done in some other way.

If my hon. friend were to visit the canal and become acquainted with the character of the work these men are doing, he would appreciate the fact that it is in the interest of the canals to have that work carried on in that way. Old gates which are partly decayed have to be renewed. This could not be done by contract. The material is purchased by tender, and is kept there properly housed and dried, so that the very best material

is used in repairing old gates and making new ones. Spare gates must necessarily be kept on band in case of accidents, because accidents do occur. Vessels going through the canals sometimes run against gates and break them, and to avoid delays it is necessary to have gates on hand ready to be put in position.
I suppose these men are discharged in the fall of the year ?
Yes.
Very nice patronage for some members along the line of the Welland canal.
I suppose that is a necessary incident of having them.
Are these men practically permanent temporaries-that is, the same skilled men kept on year after year ?
Yes. Many of them have been employed right along for years. Of course, at times, if there is a great rush, it is necessary to have additional ones.
The minister says that they not only repair gates but make new ones. In that way do they make all the gates we require, or does the government sometimes have to-buy gates ?
The gates are all made by the employees on the canal.
In purchasing supplies for the canals, I understood the minister to state that he always asked for tenders ?

The iron work in connection with these very gates is done by contract. I am speaking of the Welland canal. I may say that the valves and the hanging gear, neither of which worked satisfactorily, are being changed. The chain valve is being replaced by what is known as the butterfly valve.

What I cannot understand is that although these canals are all new, the cost of maintaining them has increased. On the Williamsburg canal the repairs last year cost $20,254, and the wages paid out amounted to $10,212. The expenditure on that canal is double what it was a few years ago when the canal was old and needed much greater repairs. Perhaps the minister can explain why the expenditure has increased so rapidly.

A new canal is much more expensive than an old canal. The new banks are much more difficult to keep in repair than old banks, because the settlement caused by time makes the latter more impervious to water and less liable to be worn away. Then, there has been a substantial increase in the wages paid.
Do these repairs extend over the whole length of the Welland canal?
Yes.
What is the length of the Welland canal ?
Twenty-seven miles.

It is a very large amount. There was spent last year on the Welland canal $85,000 or $80,000 for labour and materials. Who hires the men and sees that they do their work, and who purchases the supplies and sees that they are got at the proper rates ?

This work is entirely in charge of the superintending engineer of the canal, J. L. Weller, a very competent man. With regard to the supplies, tenders are asked for annually for all the materials required, by public advertisement, and the tenders are submitted to the department here. They come under my personal supervision, and the contracts are awarded to the lowest tenderers. Everything that is used in connection with the canal, whether tools or materials, is the subject of tender and contract.	[DOT]
What is the area of these tenders? They must be merely local, are they not?
The advertisements are quite general. Some of the successful tenderers are in St. Catharines, but parties at Hamilton, Toronto and other points also tender.

Are we to understand that the engineer employs them in connection with the Welland canal ? That is not in accord with the policy laid down by the hon. minister the other evening when he said he invariably consulted the sitting member. In this case is the sitting member not consulted?

I think my hon. friend tears something said and then puts his own interpretation upon it. I made no such statement. What I said was that in so far as patronage was concerned, if it became a question to be decided by me, I would always consult my friends ? My hon. friend is welcome to any benefit he can get from that statement. But I have to-day been asked a question regarding this particular canal, and I have said that the appointment of the officials is made by the department, but that the employment of men from time to time is done by the superintending engineer. The selection of permanent men is submitted to the department. In some cases, where it is necessary, the appointments are made by Order in Council. In others they are made by the department.

I do not wish to misrepresent the hon. gentleman, and I am quite sure he does not wdsh to misquote me, but he has misquoted me none the less. I asked the other evening the same question, namely, what the policy of his department was in

i
lespeet to the employment of men, and he gave me a straight answer, which no one could misconstrue. His answer was that the policy of his department was to consult the sitting member in the county. My hon. friend shakes his head but ' Hansard ' will prove that I am correct. The item was repairs to the Cornwall canal and the question was raised concerning the large number of men employed on that canal in election time. But this evening, in answer to the hon. member for North Toronto, (Mr. Foster) my hon. friend said that the employment of the men was in the hands of the engineer. I asked him if that was the policy of his department, and he said it was. I would like to know what is really the policy of the department in this matter.

In cases where questions arise in my department concerning the employment of men and the names are submitted to me, I say frankly that if I have the opportunity, I consult the sitting member, provided he is friendly to me and the administration. But speaking now of what has transpired in 'connection with this canal, I repeat that the superintending engineer selects the temporary men, and where permanent men are required, those recommended by our friends and who are satisfactory in other respects get the appointments.
To build retaining wall in rook cut, Welland canal, $60,000.

Improvements, Trent canal, $17,000.
What is to be done with that 7

These improvements consist of the entrance pier at Lovesick, $2,000 ; Young's Point landing pier lower entrance, $3,000 ; Young's point new swing bridge, $3,500 ; removing shoal in river below Hastings, $2,000 ; removing shoals in liver below Peterboro, $2,000; Young's point entrance to lock, $3,000 ; purchase of concrete mixture in connection with repairs to canal, $1,500.
St. Ours canal-new booms and pier, $7,300.

The present conditions for mooring are quite insufficient. In order to remedy this condition, the piers are to be extended some 200 feet. I am advised by the engineers of the department that this is a very urgent improvement. It will cost $7,300.
Repairs to guide piers, Greece's Point, $4,660; building new lighthouse, $190 ; rebuilding Grenville wharf, $23,000.
What is this for ?

These piers were built in 1880 and a portion of them require to be rebuilt. They also require a new lighthouse which will cost $190. Then the Grenville wharf will require to be rebuilt. We asked a vote of $23,000 last year but that was not expended and I am asking a revote.
That should be down as a revote.
It is a revote of $23,000.
The minister must have been very careless in framing his estimates -there are several of these errors.
They were sent to the printer by the department in proper shape.
The proof-reading is bad ?
It certainly is bad. I found a number of errors of this character.
Last year it was the same way.
Special care was taken by the officials of the department in this matter this year because I found it very embarrassing last year on several occasions when there were revotes that were not so marked.
Who does the proof-reading ?
I do not know. I suppose it is done in the Printing Bureau.
Are you making a new wharf there ?
There was a wharf there, and we are rebuilding. This is a revote from last year.
This is a large amount of money.
Is it for canal traffic ?
It has always been used in connection with canal traffic.
Was this by contract ?

Yes, the contract was given to Messrs. Martiueau & Son after public advertisement calling for tenders. The contract was made on December 5th ; no work has been done owing to the late date at which the contract was let.
Is the minister taking out the old wharf to put in the new one ?
We take out the old wharf down to water-level.
What are the dimensions of the wharf 7
It is about 300 feet long. There is a large amount of concrete work in it.

This wharf is necessary.
A wharf has been there ever since I can remember. I am glad the minister has given a contract for the work, because I see that last year, in building guide piers at the same place, the department paid for spruce and hemlock timber $30 a thousand feet, a larger sum than I have ever been able to get for it in my experience.
There was a guide-pier built last year. Can that be utilized in connection with the new work ?
The guide-pier is different from the wharf.
What has the minister to say about paying $30 a thousand for timber that a practical man says he never could get so high a price for ?
Of course, this was a year previous to my incumbency in office. I am advised by the chief engineer that all the material was purchased by tender and contract.
But if tenders are called for and all of them seem high the minister is bound not to accept any of them.
In any such cases coming under my own notice I certainly hesitate to accept any tender, and I am satisfied that is the course pursued by the department generally.
Was it because of extraordinary size of this timber that so high a rate was paid ?

The chief engineer tells me that for the kind of timber purchased $30 a thousand was not out of the way. I cannot give dimensions but I can furnish a statement later on if the hon. gentlemen desire it.
This was spruce and hemlock timber and, it was charged for at this high rate. There could have been no justification except its size and quality.
And its length.
The length I include in the size. It would need to be extraordinary in some way to be worth $30 a thousand.

I understand this would be the ordinary timber used in crib-work. I do not suppose there would be much difference between that and cribs constructed elsewhere. My recollection is that in my county where some work was done constructing a pier, hemlock timber was bought for about $17 a thousand from a mill on the Georgian bay, delivered on Lake Ontario. Certainly $30 a thousand seems to be an extraordinary price.

I think I am right in stating that this timber was bought by competition, and that was the lowest tender
for that class. It certainly could not be very much out of the way, because where there is competition the tenderers are not very apt to make the price unreasonably high if they have any hope of geting the contract.
Some departments have a peculiar way of bringing about competition. They invite two or three of their friends doing business to send in tenders.
This was done by newspaper advertisement.
As I understand, this was piling, and piling is not usually bought by the thousand feet.
I have not referred to the Auditor General's account;. Will the hon. gentleman state what kind of timber it was that we paid $30 for ?
Page 123-timber, spruce and hemlock, per thousand feet, $30. It does not say what size.
Surely the minister can tell what work was done there, whether it was piling or not.

I would call attention to this fact. The minister says he advertised for tenders. I would like to know how he managed it, because there is no newspaper in that county except one, and that is miles away from the spot. If tenders are asked for from private parties, as I understand is sometimes done, and people are asked to tender, that is one tiling entirely different from asking for tenders in a large city where newspapers are numerous.

Tenders were asked for by advertisement, as I am advised by the engineer, in the papers of Ottawa and Montreal, and in local papers if there are any in the county. That is the usual way. But it was all by newspaper advertisement.

If this was ordinary crib-work, it is the very roughest kind of timber that is used for that purpose, and the price charged here is at least double, no matter what the length, because knotty, rough timber is used generally for that purpose.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, it is usually the best timber that is used in crib-work, not rough timber. What makes the price of timber sometimes abnormally high is its length and the time of the year it has to be supplied. The time of the year it is supplied, the length of the timber, the quality of the timber, are all considerations which go to enhance the price, and it is a good quality of timber that is required for crib-work.

I do not profess to have any professional knowledge, but I understood from the minister that the work in question was the construction of a wharf on foundations that already existed there.

Therefore, I have no right to assume that the timber would be of auy extraordinary length. I would assume that the timber was like that used in my own countv. I find there was paid last year for 778' feet of hemlock $20.50, and to my mind the hemlock in the two cases would be very much similar. In one case it is $30 a thousand, in the other $20.50.

The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) says the season of the year at which the timber is procured would make a difference in the price. Granting that, it would show bad management on the part of the department if they did not procure this timber at a season of the year when it could be most cheaply procured. They waited until it could be procured only in the most expensive way. It was not a rush order. As to the length of the timber, we cannot get any information.

I will explain why it could not be bought at the proper time. In the year previous the appropriations were abnormally late, and the department cannot undertake works unless parliament has appropriated the money.
You often do it.

No. I want to say frankly to my hon. friend that we do not do it, and I have felt embarrassment on more than one occasion, and was delayed for some months in accepting tenders because the appropriations had not been voted.

I think the explanation of the minister is a lame one, because you can get timber in either winter or summer. I have bought a lot of timber and used it in building piers, both in winter and summer. The timber can be had on the spot about as cheap in one season as another.

The Minister of Agriculture will take the third reading of the Census Bill. Then we will go into supply, and the Minister of Railways will finish canals, and the acting Minister of Public Works will proceed with his estimates ; if not, the Minister of Agriculture will proceed with his.
